sources.title: Thomas Church, Jordan S. Ellenberg and Benson Farb, “FI-modules and stability for representations of symmetric groups”, arXiv:1204.4533v4 (2014); published in Duke Math. J. 164 (2015) 1833–1910
sources.locator: §1 printed pp. 2–9; §2.1–§2.3 printed pp. 10–15; §3.1–§3.4 printed pp. 16–25. Read in full in the extracted text of the 54-page PDF (arXiv:1204.4533v4, 3 November 2014); the printed page numbers are those of the published Duke article and match the design's locators (Definitions 1.1–1.4, Theorems 1.3, 1.5, 1.13, 3.3.4, 3.4.1).

contents.name: Definition 1.1 (the category FI) and Definition 1.2 (finite generation of FI-modules), printed pp. 2–3
The character-polynomial paragraph and Definition 1.4 (eventually polynomial characters), printed pp. 2–3
Introductory examples: the permutation representation has character X_1 (printed p. 3)
Introductory example: the exterior square of the permutation representation has character binom(X_1,2) − X_2 (printed p. 3)
Theorem 1.3 (Noetherian property over Noetherian rings containing Q) with its complete proof, printed pp. 3 and 20–21
Theorem 1.5 (polynomiality of characters), printed pp. 3–4
Corollary 1.6 (characters in the examples list are eventually polynomial), printed p. 4
contents.reason: Corollary 1.6 applies Theorem 1.5 to the geometric examples of Table 1; those applications are not built by this pair, and the corollary itself asserts nothing beyond the already-included Theorem 1.5 for the abstract theory.

contents.name: Remark on H^2(Mg,n) not being finitely generated, printed p. 4
contents.reason: The remark illustrates that geometric FI-modules need not be finitely generated; this page builds the abstract theory and its character-polynomial consequences, not the moduli-space examples.

contents.name: Theorem 1.7 and the FI#-module discussion (partial injections), printed pp. 4–5
contents.reason: The FI#-module structure is a strictly stronger partial-injection structure with its own rigidity theory; no claim or proof route of this page or its companion uses it, so it is deliberately not scaffolded here.

contents.name: Theorem 1.8, Theorem 1.9 and Table 1: configuration-space applications and the list of finitely generated examples, printed pp. 4–6
contents.reason: The configuration-space, moduli-space, rank-variety and Torelli applications are geometric corollaries of the FI framework; the track's deliberate limits exclude those application pages and no selected claim depends on them.

contents.name: Theorem 1.11 and the diagonal-coinvariant discussion, printed pp. 6–7
contents.reason: Diagonal coinvariant algebras form a separate application of the Noetherian theorem; neither this page nor its examples companion states or uses any coinvariant result.

contents.name: Theorem 1.13 (finite generation is equivalent to uniform representation stability) with its complete proof, printed pp. 6 and 21–23
Definitions 2.1.1–2.1.6: FI-modules, subobjects, pointwise constructions, graded modules and graded algebras, printed pp. 11–12
Definition 2.2.1 (FB-modules), Definition 2.2.2 (the free FI-module M(W)) and equation (4) for M(W)_n, printed p. 12
Definitions 2.2.3–2.2.6: M(m), the examples M(0) and M(1), the padded partition lambda[n], V(lambda)_n and M(lambda), printed p. 13
Remark 2.2.A on projective FI-modules, printed p. 13
contents.reason: Projective FI-modules and the enough-projectives statement are not used by any proof route of this pair; the construction needed here is the free module M(W) only.

contents.name: Definition 2.3.3 (generation in degree ≤ m), Definition 2.3.4 (finite generation), and the characterization in terms of M(m), printed pp. 14–15
Lemma 2.3.2 (the image of M(m) → V is the span) and Proposition 2.3.5 (finite generation via surjections from free modules), printed pp. 14–15
Proposition 2.3.6 (tensor products of finitely generated FI-modules) with proof, printed p. 14
Definition 2.3.7 (the functor H_0), Remark 2.3.8 and Remark 2.3.9 (FI-homology), printed p. 15
contents.reason: H_0 and the derived FI-homology organise generators and presentations; the local proof of Theorem 1.3 follows the weight-and-coinvariant route, and no selected claim of this pair uses H_0 or FI-homology.

contents.name: Definition 3.1.1 (graded k[T]-module), Definition 3.1.2 (the functor Phi_a) and the well-definedness of T, printed p. 16
Definition 3.1.3 (stability degree), Remark 3.1.4 and Definition 3.1.5 (injectivity and surjectivity degree), printed pp. 16–17
Lemma 3.1.6 (surjectivity degree is monotone under quotients; injectivity degree under submodules over Q-algebras), printed p. 17
Proposition 3.1.7 (injectivity and surjectivity degree of M(W)), printed p. 17
Proposition 3.1.8 (generated in degree ≤ d implies surjectivity degree ≤ d) and the following sharpness paragraph, printed p. 17
Definition 3.2.1 (weight of an FI-module), printed p. 18
Proposition 3.2.2 (weight of a tensor product is at most the sum of weights), printed p. 18
contents.reason: The subadditivity weight(V⊗W) ≤ weight(V)+weight(W) is not used by any proof on this page; it is the natural quantitative input when tensor products of irreducible families are bounded on the Murnaghan page, which is the planned consumer of this pair.

contents.name: Lemma 3.2.3 (branching rule for S_n-representations), printed p. 18
Proposition 3.2.4 (weight of M(\u00b5) equals |\u00b5|), printed p. 18
Proposition 3.2.5 (generated in degree ≤ d implies weight ≤ d), printed p. 19
Proposition 3.2.6 (stability degree of M(lambda) equals lambda_1), printed p. 19
Lemma 3.2.7 (coinvariants of padded irreducibles: vanishing, boundary, stabilisation and detection), printed pp. 18–19
Proposition 3.2.8 (the stability degree bounds the first row of every constituent), printed p. 20
Remark 3.3.1 (not every consistent sequence comes from an FI-module), printed p. 21
Definition 3.3.2 (uniform representation stability; injectivity, spanning and multiplicities), printed p. 21
Proposition 3.3.3 (weight and stability degree give uniform representation stability in degrees ≥ weight + stability degree) with complete proof, printed pp. 21–22
Theorem 3.3.4 (polynomiality of characters: existence, degree bound and uniqueness) with complete proof, printed pp. 23–24
Proposition 3.4.1 (the FI-module V(lambda) realising one padded irreducible family) with complete proof, printed pp. 24–25
Theorem 3.4.2 (Murnaghan's theorem for tensor products of padded irreducibles), printed p. 25
contents.reason: Murnaghan's theorem on tensor products of padded irreducible families is exactly the subject of the planned Murnaghan page (batch 28), which consumes this pair; scaffolding it here would duplicate the later page's theorem.

contents.name: Propositions 3.4.3 and 3.4.5 and Corollary 3.4.4 (stability for Schur functors), printed p. 25
contents.reason: Stability of Schur functors is not a promised claim of the selected 24-pair scope and no item of this pair or its companion uses Schur functors; the design's deliberate limits exclude this direction.

sources.title: Thomas Church, Jordan S. Ellenberg, Benson Farb and Rohit Nagpal, “FI-modules over Noetherian rings”, Geom. Topol. 18 (2014) 2951–2984; author-hosted full text
sources.locator: §1 printed pp. 1–9 (Theorems A, B, C, D–F, Corollary 1.4, Remarks 1.1–1.9) and §2.1–§2.2 printed pp. 9–16 (Definitions 2.1–2.11, Lemmas 2.5–2.6, Proposition 2.12, Corollary 2.13, and the proof of Theorem A). Read in the extracted text of the 31-page author-hosted PDF.

contents.name: Theorem A (Noetherian property: sub-FI-modules of finitely generated FI-modules over any Noetherian ring are finitely generated), printed pp. 1–2
Theorem B (polynomial dimension over any field) and Remark 1.2, printed pp. 1–3
contents.reason: Positive-characteristic and integral dimension polynomiality is a different regime; this pair is deliberately characteristic-zero and its dimension corollary is derived from the character polynomial, not from Theorem B.

contents.name: Theorem C (inductive description/central stability), printed p. 1
contents.reason: Central stability in the sense of Putman is a different formulation of the stability conclusion; neither the pair's statements nor its proof routes use inductive descriptions.

contents.name: Corollary 1.4 (finitely generated FI-modules over a Noetherian ring form an abelian category), printed p. 3
contents.reason: The abelian-category consequence is not needed: the local Noetherian theorem is stated and used as a finite-generation statement, and the pair never quantifies over the abelian category of finitely generated FI-modules.

contents.name: Theorems D–F and Theorems 1.5–1.6, 1.10–1.13 (congruence subgroups, configuration spaces, coinvariant algebras), printed pp. 3–9
contents.reason: These are the paper's applications of the Noetherian property in topology, number theory and commutative algebra; they lie outside the selected representation-theory scope and no selected claim depends on them.

contents.name: Definition 2.1 (finitely generated FI-modules), Definition 2.2 (free FI-modules M(d)) and Proposition 2.3 (characterization of finite generation), printed pp. 9–10
Definition 2.4 (H_0), Lemma 2.5 (H_0 detects zero and surjections) and Lemma 2.6 (generation criteria), printed pp. 10–12
contents.reason: H_0 is the source's tool for the shift-functor proof; the local scaffold follows the characteristic-zero weight route to Theorem 1.3, and no selected claim uses H_0.

contents.name: Definitions 2.7–2.11 (positive shift functors, the morphisms X_a, and the relation ∼) with Proposition 2.12 and Corollary 2.13, printed pp. 12–14
contents.reason: The positive-shift machinery is the source's alternative proof of the Noetherian property over arbitrary rings; it was read to corroborate Theorem A but is not scaffolded because the local proof follows the weight argument and no selected claim uses shift functors.

contents.name: The proof of Theorem A via shift functors, printed pp. 12–16
contents.reason: This is the second, independent proof route for the same Noetherian statement; it is recorded as corroborating evidence for the local theorem but not rebuilt as separate items on this page.

Chapter I §7 Example 14, uniqueness clause: two character polynomials agreeing on S_n for infinitely many n coincide, printed pp. 123–124
